one_line: Agent-operated hackathon administration across event workflows.
what_it_does: Lets organizers manage hackathon events, submissions, judging, attendees, and notifications from an agent rather than juggling multiple admin interfaces.
leverage_rationale: WebMCP makes a broad, stateful admin workflow available through structured tools, including status queries and actions that are cumbersome across Devpost, spreadsheets, and email. The packet still provides only claimed end-to-end capability, so this is not scored transformative.
leverage_evidence: Pitch explicitly replaces multiple organizer interfaces with agent access.
Devpost packaging visibly shows event sections for challenges, teams, people, judging, and action items.
About text describes querying signups, starting judging, retrieving projects, and sending mass notifications.
execution_rationale: The submission is coherent and the packaging plus embedded demo thumbnail show a substantial organizer dashboard, but there is no submitted video frame sheet and no transcript; end-to-end execution is only partially evidenced.
execution_evidence: Devpost screenshot shows hackathon.new dashboard with event-management sections.
Visible demo packaging includes status such as 8 of 19 complete and ready to start judging.
Facts report a live demo link but no video evidence was submitted in the packet.
impact_rationale: Hackathon organizers and volunteers have a concrete multi-system coordination problem, and the proposed workflow directly targets it.
impact_evidence: Author reports running about two dozen hackathons yearly.
Pitch identifies spreadsheet, Notion, Devpost, judging, prizes, and attendee coordination as the problem.
Solution targets non-technical volunteers as well as organizers.
creativity_rationale: Applying WebMCP to end-to-end hackathon operations is a fresh and ambitious workflow synthesis, though the underlying admin functions are familiar.
creativity_evidence: Agent-first operation of a full hackathon lifecycle is the central concept.
The project bridges event administration, judging, project retrieval, and communications.
usability_note: The stated goal is simpler than learning several admin systems, but usability beyond the dashboard is not directly observed.
red_flags: No submitted video frame sheets or transcript; execution evidence is packaging-heavy.
standouts: Clear real-world organizer workflow and strong agent-centered rationale.
advance_reason: Strong impact and leverage case with coherent packaging, despite thin direct execution evidence.

one_line: A shared shopping mission board where an agent assembles multi-store kits and humans approve choices.
what_it_does: Parses a shopping mission, plans a budgeted kit, searches products across Shopify merchants, incorporates locks and rejections, and prepares merchant checkout links.
leverage_rationale: The product depends on structured, shared live state: the agent plans and searches while the human locks or rejects items and the agent replans without losing decisions. That collaboration is materially harder through generic UI driving.
leverage_evidence: Frame sheets show staged create_mission, plan_kit, search_products, choose_candidate, and checkout workflow.
Transcript explicitly describes human locks/rejections being carried into replanning.
Transcript states tool changes, shared edits, and one real cart link per merchant.
execution_rationale: The video transcript and frame sheets cover the central workflow from mission creation through product selection and checkout preparation, with visible product cards and human approval states. Minor uncertainty remains around live merchant execution.
execution_evidence: Frames show product search cards, selection/rejection states, and checkout preparation.
Transcript reports a $373.17 kit across seven merchants and links to merchant checkouts.
Devpost packaging identifies WebMCP and real Shopify checkouts.
impact_rationale: Cross-store shopping missions are a real, repeated problem for outdoor trips, home setups, and similar kits; the product addresses budget, constraints, and preferences directly.
impact_evidence: Camping request visibly includes budget, owned gear, and sleep preference.
Transcript gives concrete use cases including backpacking, espresso setups, and first apartments.
The board preserves user decisions instead of forcing a restart.
creativity_rationale: The shared human-agent shopping board, staged tool disclosure, and persistent human decisions are a notably original interaction model for commerce.
creativity_evidence: Frames depict tool stages and tool-change events as part of the interaction.
Human locks and rejects are represented as first-class planning state.
Multi-merchant kit planning and checkout links are pursued as one coherent experience.
usability_note: The board makes agent actions and human approvals visible, while checkout remains user-controlled; the multi-merchant flow may still be complex.
standouts: Strongest evidence of shared live state and meaningful human-agent collaboration.
End-to-end commerce flow is unusually well demonstrated.
advance_reason: Exceptional WebMCP leverage with strong demonstrated execution, impact, and originality.

one_line: Human-approved AI recovery workflow for manufacturing incidents.
what_it_does: Investigates a supplier delay, finds affected orders and inventory, compares suppliers, proposes a recovery plan, requests approval, and executes it through an operations dashboard.
leverage_rationale: Structured tools let an agent query multiple operational entities and execute only after human approval, avoiding brittle navigation across incident, inventory, order, and supplier screens.
leverage_evidence: Devpost screenshot visibly includes a WebMCP tool inspector beside the incident dashboard.
About text lists incident, orders, inventory, supplier search, recovery plan, approval, execution, and final status tools.
Shared dashboard state and approval boundary are explicit.
execution_rationale: The packaging clearly shows a coherent incident dashboard with a concrete scenario and tool inspector, but no frame sheet or transcript demonstrates the full recovery execution.
execution_evidence: Visible dashboard shows constrained production, three orders at risk, critical material, and R423,000 impact.
Visible incident states a supplier delivery delayed 48 hours and a blocked job.
Packet has a live demo but no submitted video evidence.
impact_rationale: Manufacturing disruption recovery has a specific audience, costly cascading consequences, and a direct operational use case; the proposed workflow addresses investigation and controlled remediation.
impact_evidence: Concrete aluminum shortage scenario affects production and customer orders.
Dashboard quantifies three jobs, three orders, and R423,000 exposed revenue.
Human approval is appropriate for consequential operational actions.
creativity_rationale: The human-guided incident-recovery framing is a strong application of agent tools to operations, though incident dashboards and approval workflows are established patterns.
creativity_evidence: Combines investigation, option comparison, approval, and execution in one agent workflow.
Explicitly uses the same data/state for human dashboard and agent tools.
usability_note: The dashboard communicates severity and approval state clearly; actual operator usability is not directly observed.
red_flags: Full end-to-end agent recovery is claimed but not directly evidenced by submitted frames or transcript.
standouts: Concrete high-stakes scenario with quantified operational impact and an approval gate.
advance_reason: High-impact, credible operations use case with strong WebMCP rationale; direct execution evidence is incomplete but sufficient to advance.

one_line: Shared live-map grid dispatch for locating, assessing, and routing field work.
what_it_does: Loads work orders against a real electricity grid, resolves transformers and affected assets, computes impact and routes, and lets a dispatcher decide with an agent on the same map.
leverage_rationale: WebMCP exposes domain-level grid lookups, impact analysis, and routing over a shared map, replacing thousands of precise spatial queries that generic UI automation would handle unreliably.
leverage_evidence: About text states 27 WebMCP tools and one-query placement of work orders against 8,676 transformers.
Frame sheets visibly show changing map views, overlays, side panels, and result data.
Pitch explicitly divides agent locating/computation/routing from human decision-making.
execution_rationale: The packet provides coherent map-based product evidence and a detailed domain workflow, but no video transcript and only low-resolution frames make exact end-to-end completion difficult to verify.
execution_evidence: Frame sheets show an interactive geospatial dashboard with map overlays, controls, and data panels.
Devpost screenshot shows a map interface with routes and markers.
About text specifies ingestion, transformer resolution, impact analysis, and three-crew routing.
impact_rationale: Utility dispatchers have a concrete, consequential daily workflow involving public-service reliability and large volumes of spatial data; the demonstrated fit is strong.
impact_evidence: Author describes hundreds of Lima work orders against a published grid.
Use case includes customers, schools, clinics, interruption hours, and regulatory tolerance.
The product targets a real dispatcher workflow rather than a generic map demo.
creativity_rationale: Applying a shared agent-human map to electricity-grid dispatch and regulatory impact analysis is an original, ambitious domain application.
creativity_evidence: Combines open grid data, work-order intake, transformer topology, impact analysis, and crew routing.
The human-agent division is purpose-built around dispatcher decisions.
usability_note: The map and side panels provide a plausible dispatcher workspace, though fine controls are hard to assess from the frames.
red_flags: Agent invocation is not directly legible in the low-resolution frame sheets.
standouts: Deep domain specificity and unusually strong spatial-data leverage.
advance_reason: High leverage and impact with credible domain depth; execution evidence is visual but not fully legible.

one_line: A shared canvas for sketching UI flows with an agent.
what_it_does: Lets users arrange interface frames, connect navigation, inspect a structured sketch, and prototype the flow while an agent reads and edits the live artifact.
leverage_rationale: The agent receives structured frames, elements, notes, flows, and selection state and can make precise edits without interpreting screenshots or exported files; the shared canvas is central.
leverage_evidence: About text specifies two native tools: napkin_describe and an edit tool, with structured active-sketch state.
Frames show a visual editor, responsive views, selected elements, and a rendered flow.
Devpost screenshot visibly shows IdeaFrame, FlowMap, RoughDraft, and an agent-driven button change.
execution_rationale: The screenshots show a coherent editor with a landing-page flow, form, responsive views, and an agent interaction, but the packet lacks a transcript and detailed end-to-end tool trace.
execution_evidence: Frames show editor canvas, component palette, selected elements, and rendered webpage preview.
Devpost media visibly includes a header, Book a Tour button, Lead Form, and registration controls.
About text describes autosave, import/export, tracing, snapshots, and three connected views.
impact_rationale: Product designers and developers have a real need to preserve visual intent and validate flows before coding; the tool credibly addresses that gap.
impact_evidence: About text identifies screenshot/prompt translation as the problem.
FlowMap and RoughDraft support planning and lightweight testing before production code.
Structured inspection reduces stale or incomplete descriptions.
creativity_rationale: The combination of spatial sketching, flow mapping, runnable rough drafts, and shared agent edits is a fresh interaction model for early product design.
creativity_evidence: Three connected views make the artifact both visual and navigable.
Agent works on the active canvas instead of a detached prompt or exported file.
usability_note: The separate views and visible preview support a clear workflow, though complexity may rise as sketches grow.
red_flags: Direct tool-call evidence is limited in the packet.
standouts: Good shared-artifact framing and clear visual design workflow.
advance_reason: Strong leverage and creative interaction with credible product evidence.

one_line: A geometry-aware viewer that exposes precise technical drawing semantics to agents.
what_it_does: Lets humans view technical drawings while agents summarize layers, inspect objects, retrieve geometry, measure distances, test intersections, and query spatial relationships.
leverage_rationale: Structured geometry tools replace unreliable screenshot interpretation and toolbar automation with deterministic domain queries. The intended agent capability is impractical from pixels alone.
leverage_evidence: About text lists seven focused tools for geometry, measurement, intersection, containment, adjacency, and hypothetical evaluation.
Frame sheets show floor-plan geometry, layers, annotations, and connectivity/analysis views.
Devpost packaging explicitly contrasts precise geometry with screenshots.
execution_rationale: The packet coherently demonstrates a viewer and geometry-focused workflow, but the low-resolution frames do not prove every claimed query end-to-end.
execution_evidence: Frames show imported architectural floor plans with rooms, walls, dimensions, layers, and analysis outputs.
Visible overlays state geometry/layers/text without a building model and show a Room Connectivity Graph.
Devpost screenshot shows branded Precidra Viewer and real dimension annotations.
impact_rationale: Architects, engineers, and technical drawing users have a real need for exact spatial reasoning; deterministic measurements and relationships are valuable beyond visual description.
impact_evidence: Technical drawings contain exact dimensions and topology that screenshots obscure.
Examples include room adjacency, obstacle distance, containment, and proposed-shape intersection.
Read-only design appropriately supports human verification.
creativity_rationale: Exposing existing CAD-like geometry directly to agents is a distinctive and technically ambitious alternative to vision-only document understanding.
creativity_evidence: Domain-level spatial predicates are the core interaction, not generic image captioning.
Human visual verification and agent geometric reasoning are deliberately separated.
usability_note: Read-only inspection and deterministic results support trust, though technical drawing workflows may require domain expertise.
red_flags: Tool invocation itself is not clearly visible in the supplied low-resolution sheets.
standouts: Exceptional WebMCP indispensability for exact geometry and spatial relations.
advance_reason: Highly differentiated agent capability with strong impact and clear visual product evidence.

one_line: A presentation editor where humans and agents edit the same slide deck.
what_it_does: Creates and modifies slides, changes themes, and inserts metric cards through structured WebMCP tools on a shared presentation canvas.
leverage_rationale: Structured slide operations are more reliable than UI driving and support shared state, but a general agent or presentation API could achieve much of the same outcome with friction.
leverage_evidence: Devpost screenshot shows Agent Inspector, tools, activity, connected status, and named slide operations.
About text identifies create, modify, theme, and metric-card tools.
Shared canvas and live human-agent collaboration are the product premise.
execution_rationale: The packaging clearly shows a presentation editor and tool inspector, but no frame sheet or video transcript was submitted, so end-to-end execution remains claimed.
execution_evidence: Screenshot shows a slide canvas, thumbnails, editor controls, and Agent Inspector.
Visible slide is titled AI-Native Workflows and includes WebMCP Powered branding.
Facts indicate a live demo and public repository, but direct run evidence is absent from the packet.
impact_rationale: Presentation creators and teams have a real need for rapid slide editing and data-driven content; shared agent operation offers credible value.
impact_evidence: Product targets a familiar collaborative presentation workflow.
Metric-card insertion and theme/content editing address concrete deck tasks.
Human and agent editing the same deck can reduce translation overhead.
creativity_rationale: Real-time human-agent co-editing is a useful synthesis, but presentation editing with structured tools is a moderately familiar category.
creativity_evidence: Agent Inspector makes tool actions visible in the editor.
Combines slide transformation and data cards with a shared canvas.
usability_note: The editor and activity inspector make actions inspectable, though the packet does not show interaction quality across states.
red_flags: No submitted video frame sheets; execution is primarily one packaging screenshot.
standouts: Visible Agent Inspector and named structured slide tools.
advance_reason: Credible shared-editor concept with visible tool integration, though evidence is thin and novelty is moderate.

one_line: A shareable itinerary whose URL grants an agent scoped read or write access.
what_it_does: Maintains a live map itinerary, gives edit links write tools and view links read-only tools, and lets an agent add, inspect, and revise travel plans in context.
leverage_rationale: WebMCP is used as a permission and shared-context surface: URL sharing changes the available tool set, while map view and itinerary state inform agent actions. This is substantially beyond UI convenience.
leverage_evidence: About text states edit links expose 12 tools and view links expose 8 read-only tools.
It describes server-enforced permission split and link rotation for revocation.
Frames and packaging show map itinerary, chat interaction, and visible edit mode/tool count.
execution_rationale: Frame sheets and transcript-free packaging still show a coherent map/chat workflow, while the about text details permissions, live facts, activity log, and route drawing. Direct video transcript is absent, so some execution remains claimed.
execution_evidence: Frames show map changes, markers, assistant panel, and itinerary states.
Devpost screenshot visibly shows Nasu/Nikko itinerary, dates, map, and edit-mode tool count.
About text specifies write/read-only links, current view, search, travel time, route drawing, and activity logging.
impact_rationale: Families and groups planning trips need shared, editable itineraries with controlled permissions; the product directly addresses collaboration and stale travel facts.
impact_evidence: The itinerary stores stops, stay times, travel slots, route notes, and wishlist items.
Live travel time and next-stop status are computed on demand.
URL sharing avoids an OAuth-heavy setup for casual collaborators.
creativity_rationale: Using URL-scoped WebMCP tool disclosure as the sharing and permission model, combined with map-contextual agent actions, is highly original and memorable.
creativity_evidence: Read-only versus write tool worlds are distinct rather than rejected after the fact.
Every call pans the map, opens a popup, and appends to an activity log.
The concept has a focused, coherent interaction model with no edit UI.
usability_note: No-edit UI and visible activity confirmation are elegant, while link permissions make collaboration understandable; map complexity remains a consideration.
red_flags: No transcript and agent invocation details are not directly readable in all frames.
standouts: Permission-scoped tool disclosure through shared URLs is a standout WebMCP-native design.
advance_reason: Highly original WebMCP permission/context model with strong product and impact evidence.

one_line: A collaborative whiteboard where people and agents brainstorm visibly together.
what_it_does: Provides a shared board for notes, connections, comments, challenges, and visual maps, with structured agent actions and an activity trail.
leverage_rationale: Structured board tools and visible agent contributions improve shared context and transparency, but generic agent interaction could reproduce much of the workflow with friction.
leverage_evidence: About text says agents inspect and act on the live canvas through structured WebMCP tools.
Devpost screenshot shows a collaborative board demo with start-session and explore-demo actions.
Visible concept emphasizes an activity trail and bounded actions.
execution_rationale: The submission is coherent as a whiteboard concept and the packaging shows a board-oriented demo, but there are no submitted frame sheets and the packet does not directly demonstrate agent actions or completion.
execution_evidence: Devpost screenshot shows a product landing/demo board with colored notes and collaboration messaging.
About text claims working shared canvas, autonomous contributions, structured tools, and activity trail.
Facts report a live demo and public repository, but visual execution evidence is packaging only.
impact_rationale: Brainstorming teams and solo creators have a real desire for visible, constructive AI participation; a shared visual board is a credible fit.
impact_evidence: Product targets brainstorming, idea mapping, comments, and assumption challenges.
About text identifies the limitation of AI as a detached chat panel.
Visible landing copy frames AI as another mind in the room.
creativity_rationale: The visible-teammate framing and bounded visual contributions are a fresh angle on whiteboards, though collaborative canvases are an established category.
creativity_evidence: Agent contributions are intended to be visible on the board rather than hidden in chat.
The project shifts from inconsistent freehand generation to deterministic diagrams.
usability_note: Visible actions and a shared board could support trust, but interaction quality and state handling are not directly evidenced.
red_flags: No frame sheets; agent behavior and end-to-end workflow are not independently visible.
standouts: Clear human-visible AI teammate concept and bounded-action rationale.
advance_reason: Promising concept and audience fit, but evidence is too thin to support advancing over better-demonstrated projects.

one_line: A WebMCP robot interface for agents to observe and control a simulated arm.
what_it_does: Lets an agent view a robot camera, read arm state, move joints, and iteratively attempt manipulation tasks in a browser simulation.
leverage_rationale: Structured low-level control and camera observation let an agent operate a robot simulation through domain actions rather than clicking controls; the physical-world extension is ambitious even though the submitted version is simulated.
leverage_evidence: About text specifies camera, arm information, joint movement, and iterative observation/action.
Frame sheets visibly show a robot arm, end effector, scene objects, and changing simulation states.
Devpost screenshot identifies WebMCP tools for robot control.
execution_rationale: The frame sheets show a coherent simulated robot interface and apparent changing object states, but text and exact task completion are not legible and no transcript is provided.
execution_evidence: Repeated frames show teal articulated arm, end effector, platform, and pink objects.
Devpost screenshot shows controls labeled Ready, Edit scene, Connect agent, View, Control, and Camera.
About text says the web version is a lightweight simulation adapted from physical-robot work.
impact_rationale: Robotics learners and experimenters have real value in accessible agent-control sandboxes; the project offers a concrete way to test embodied tool use.
impact_evidence: Author explicitly targets experimentation with models controlling robots.
Simulation avoids requiring physical hardware while retaining camera/action loop.
Users can try prompts and compare agent behavior.
creativity_rationale: Combining WebMCP with embodied visual feedback and iterative robot manipulation is ambitious and more distinctive than a standard chatbot demo.
creativity_evidence: Agent is denied hidden object positions and must observe, act, and adjust.
The project bridges prior physical arm experiments into an accessible web simulation.
usability_note: The explicit View/Control/Camera surfaces suggest understandable experimentation, but the low-resolution evidence makes the actual task UX uncertain.
red_flags: Submitted web version is a simulation rather than the physical robot described in the inspiration; exact successful task completion is unclear.
standouts: Embodied observe-act-adjust loop and refusal to expose hidden object positions.
advance_reason: Strong technical ambition and meaningful agent-control delta with visible simulation evidence.
